name: PT Golden Eagle Energy Tbk

frontmatter.title: Golden Eagle Energy — a low-grade, long-haul thermal producer priced past its cycle
frontmatter.summary: Golden Eagle Energy is a small Indonesian thermal-coal producer whose sub-bituminous coal and long road haul set its realised price at a fraction of the seaborne benchmark. This revision answers the red team: the post-2030 licence tail is carried at a sourced extension probability, the associate is marked down for its lapsed permit, and the realised price is stressed in the bear case. The shares still sit on a thin free float at many times our through-cycle value, so SELL holds.
thesis: We stay at SELL with a target of Rp1,615 against a price of Rp3,100, a total return of -46.9%.

The variant view is grade and logistics, not price direction: Triaryani's coal is a sub-bituminous product around 4,100 kcal/kg GAR whose realised price has run at roughly a third of the Newcastle marker, and the road haul to the Lalan terminal is the single largest cost line in the P&L [S3] [S2].

At the coal deck's through-cycle Newcastle marker the mine's cash margin is a handful of dollars a tonne, so free cash flow is close to zero even after we strip the development capex out of the run rate [S3].
The market is not paying for through-cycle cash flow; today's price requires the seaborne benchmark to run at a multiple of the deck's forward path to be justified [S0].

The price is a regime price, not a fundamental one: at 9.7 times our fundamental value the house konglo lens holds part of that premium for twelve months, which is why the target is Rp1,615 against a fundamental value of Rp318 [S0] [S7].

The bull case is real and we state it: a sustained war-premium bid in seaborne coal, a lifted RKAB quota, a wider third-party sales mix and a renewal of the mine licence past the end of the decade at a sourced extension probability would together change the arithmetic [S6] [S13].

blocks.text: This note replaces the 27 October 2026 initiation, which was withdrawn while the name was re-run under the house's konglo regime lens. Three things changed in this revision and they are all fundamental, not cosmetic. First, the mine's post-2030 licence tail is no longer valued at zero: the 314 Mt reserve beyond the 2030 operating permit is carried at a sourced extension probability, the way this house treats the equivalent tail at MCOL [S13] [S12]. Second, the associate is marked down from its carrying value because its own permit has expired and it produced nothing this year [S2] [S6]. Third, the realised price — which is calibrated on a related-party contract — is now stressed in the bear case [S3]. What the lens adds on top is the regime step. SMMT is a konglo name in the regime sense — the listed vehicle of a Singapore-controlled coal group, on the exchange's high-shareholding-concentration list, with a free float below the new statutory floor — and the house lens sets the twelve-month target as the fundamental value times the share of today's premium the regime keeps over the window. That is **Rp1,615** against a fundamental value of Rp318, because the price sits at 9.7 times value and the base regime keeps most of that gap rather than closing it. The rating is unchanged at **SELL**: the price is many times what the asset is worth on our own numbers even after the regime step.

We cover PT Golden Eagle Energy Tbk (SMMT) at **SELL** with a twelve-month target of **Rp1,615** versus a last price of Rp3,100, a total return of -46.9%. The company is a small Indonesian thermal-coal producer that sells a sub-bituminous product from one operating concession in South Sumatra and holds an indirect minority in a second mine in East Kalimantan that is operating but idle this year [S2] [S6]. Its coal is low-rank and its mine is a long road haul from the barging terminal, so its realised price ran at roughly a third of the Newcastle benchmark in the last audited year and its cost base is dominated by haulage, barging and jetty handling rather than by the coal-getting itself [S3] [S2]. The company has just re-rated sharply: the shares rose by roughly three-quarters in the month to end-September 2026, the exchange flagged unusual market activity and then suspended trading for cooling down, and management's own incidental public expose attributes the move mainly to transaction volume and to the index price rather than to a change in the business [S5] [S6].

Our variant view is not about the coal price. It is that the market is capitalising this asset on the seaborne benchmark while the company's own realised price is a small fraction of it, and that the mine's through-cycle cash margin is thin enough that free cash flow is close to zero even after we remove the one-off development spend that inflated the last two years' capex [S3]. Working from the coal deck's reviewed through-cycle marker, the calibrated realisation and the rate the accounts show being paid in royalty, the life-of-asset DCF is worth only Rp168 against today's price. The three things that move the value are the seaborne benchmark path, the annual RKAB quota that caps volume, and the haulage cost per tonne — the last of which the company has been investing to relieve through its Lalan river terminal and its own barge ports [S2].

We are not bearish by default. The bull case is explicit and is carried in the scenarios: a sustained war-premium bid in seaborne thermal coal, an RKAB quota lifted toward the company's own plan, a wider third-party sales mix and a little more volume would together lift realised price and margin. The licence tail and the associate's restart are separate, dated optionality we carry in the bridge and the signposts, not in the scenario shocks. A reader who believes the benchmark stays near spot rather than reverting to the deck should own this name; a reader who believes the deck should not.

Golden Eagle Energy began life as an entertainment company and only moved into coal mining in this
century, taking over a South Sumatran concession that has been producing since the middle of the
last decade. It is controlled by a Singapore-listed coal group whose regional office sits in
Jakarta, and its shares carry a very small free float, which makes the tape thin and prone to large
moves on modest flow. Sub-bituminous Indonesian coal of this rank is sold mainly to power stations
and cement plants in Asia, so demand tracks electricity generation and industrial activity rather
than the steel cycle.

Golden Eagle Energy is a coal-mining holding company. Its product reaches the market through PT Triaryani, a wholly-owned subsidiary that holds an IUP Operasi Produksi over a concession in the Musi Rawas Utara regency of South Sumatra and has been operating since the middle of the last decade [S2]. A second mine, PT Internasional Prima Coal in Palaran, East Kalimantan, is held as a forty-nine per cent associate through PT Mega Raya Kusuma and is therefore equity-accounted rather than consolidated [S2] [S6]. That distinction matters for anyone modelling the group: the income statement carries only Triaryani's revenue, while the group's headline operating statistics in the annual report include the associate's tonnes [S2]. The associate is not a shell: it is an operating mine with a higher-rank product than Triaryani's, holding an IUP over a large concession in East Kalimantan with its own haul road and barging ports [S2]. It produced 0.7 Mt and sold 0.7 Mt in the last audited year and sold close to a million tonnes the year before, and it paid the group US$2.1m of cash dividends in the last audited year [S2] [S3]. What it is is idle: it produced nothing at all in the current year while its licence ran down, and management blames the associate's absence for part of the group's output decline [S6]. So it is a real, cash-generative asset that is switched off, not a dormant one — it sold 0.7 Mt in the last audited year, close to a million tonnes the year before, and paid the group cash dividends US$2.1m [S2] [S3]. It is worth no more than its book in the base case for a specific reason: its IUP Operasi Produksi expired in 2026 [S2], so we mark the stake to its share of the associate's own net assets rather than to the carrying premium the accounts show, and we hold the restart as an unbooked option [S3]. The valuation section sets out that mark-down and the value it removes.

The product is thermal coal, and its rank is the heart of the investment case. Triaryani's coal carries a calorific value of about 4,100 kcal/kg GAR with low sulphur and low ash, and the company's own public-expose material describes the product as clean and homogeneous at a rank in the low four-thousands [S2] [S6]. The associate's coal is a materially higher-rank product [S2]. Both are open-pit operations; the group reports a single reportable segment, coal mining, and a single geographic area, Indonesia, so there is no segment split to manage [S3].

Strategically the company is a capacity builder rather than a consolidator. Its stated levers are to raise the production target inside the annual work plan and budget while respecting the logistics constraint of its coal haul road, to add haulage fleet and improve port loading, and to widen its market through long-term contracts while protecting coal quality to hold the selling price [S2]. The haulage route is the binding constraint: coal travels by road to a terminal on the Lalan river and then barges out, and the company has been adding road, jetty and barge-port infrastructure rather than buying tonnes [S2]. Management has also been restructuring the group's holding chain, moving its stake in the associate through a holding vehicle and buying the remaining interest in one of its intermediate holding companies in the last audited year [S3] [S6].

On competitive position the company is a challenger, not a leader. Its concession is small against the state producer or the large private coal names, it reports a single mine's worth of reserves rather than a portfolio, and it has no metallurgical coal, no downstream smelter and no branded product [S2]. The group employed a small workforce at the last count and has no institutionally-held float to speak of, with public shareholders holding a low-double-digit share of the register and the controlling shareholder holding the balance [S0].

Indonesian thermal coal is a mature, policy-shaped export industry. National production fell in the last completed year, the government's own reference price for high-calorie coal fell by roughly a fifth across that year, and the director general's published expectation for the coming year's national production target is lower again on softer demand from the main export destinations [S2]. Domestic consumption takes a large slice of national output through the domestic market obligation, with the balance exported or carried into stock [S2]. For a producer of this size, the binding constraints are therefore not market share but the annual government work plan and budget, known as the RKAB, which caps how much a concession may produce, and the US dollar reference prices the government sets twice a month [S2] [S6].

The coal deck is the driver we underwrite against. Its reviewed marker for high-rank seaborne thermal coal is a forecast path that starts above the last realised year, steps down through the middle of the decade and settles at a long-run level, with the deck explicitly flagging that spot sits well above the forward path as a war-premium carry rather than a level it expects to persist US$137/t US$118/t US$105/t. The government's own high-calorie reference price and the domestic power cap bracket the product set, and the deck's lower-rank reference prices for mid- and low-calorie grades show how steeply value declines with rank US$127/t US$70.0/t US$66.1/t. The deck's read on Indonesia's supply discipline and the demand outlook is the backdrop we work to [S2].

That grade ladder is our whole competitive read. A producer at the top of the rank ladder can realise close to the seaborne benchmark; a producer at Triaryani's rank realises a fraction of it, and then hands a further slice of the delivered price to the road haul, the barge, the jetty and the transshipment step before the coal reaches a vessel [S3]. Coal of this rank also competes with domestic mine-mouth supply for the power plants, and the domestic market obligation caps what those tonnes can earn at the government's power price rather than at export parity [S2].

On the five forces, buyer concentration is the practical constraint: a very large share of group revenue is a sale to a single related party within the controlling shareholder's group, under a coal sales and purchase agreement alongside a marketing-services agreement with the same counterparty [S3]. Suppliers are fewer than they look, because much of the cost base is contracted haulage and barging rather than a competitive commodity input [S3]. Related-party gravity runs through the cost side as well as the revenue side, and round one understated it. The logistics that carry the largest cost line — the haul road and the jetty — are provided by PT Marga Bara Jaya, an affiliate of the same controlling group, and the group funds that build through advances booked as other non-current assets [S3 note 17, note 34]. On the accounts' own cost-of-sales split, hauling is US$48.0m and jetty and loading a further US$8.0m [S3 note 28], together the majority of the cost of sales, so a large part of the cost base is contracted with an entity inside the controlling shareholder's group. Read the other way, the marketing-services fee the same group charges on the sales side, US$1.8m, is under a dollar a tonne off the realised price [S3 note 29, note 34]. We are precise about what is disclosed and what is not: the filing does not name the counterparty of the haulage charge line itself, and the one supplier it discloses above a tenth of sales is a third party [S3 note 28], so the related-party cost exposure is real but cannot be sized to the last dollar from the notes. A member of the board is also the president director of that logistics affiliate, which we note as a governance fact rather than a financing one [S2]. Barriers to entry are high on paper, since mining permits are not freely available, but they protect an incumbent that is still subscale and high-cost, which is a weak moat in practice [S2]. Substitution risk over the long run comes from the energy transition, which the company itself flags as its central sustainability challenge, and from the electrification of the mine fleet it says it is exploring [S2]. Regulation is the swing force: royalties, the domestic market obligation, export-proceeds retention rules and the frequency with which the RKAB quota is reset all move the economics of a marginal tonne more than they move a first-quartile one [S2] [S6].

The last audited year was a year of growth with almost no margin. Consolidated revenue doubled, but cost of sales rose by nearly the same amount, so gross profit was only a thin slice of sales and operating profit was marginal once general and administrative costs were taken 103.6 95.2 8.4 4.3. Reported net profit was small but larger than operating profit, because the group's share of the associate's earnings, a foreign-exchange gain and interest income all sat below the operating line [S3]. The cost of sales note is the most revealing page in the filing: haulage alone is the largest line, followed by barging, overburden removal, jetty and loading, then depreciation and amortisation, then the government royalty [S3]. Coal-getting proper is a minor item. This is a logistics business with a mine attached.

Volume is the swing factor, and the reported series is volatile. Triaryani sold roughly a million tonnes two years ago, then around two and a half million in the last audited year, and the company's own plan for the current year names a volume target well above that, paired with a revenue target that implies a materially higher realised price [S2]. We do not carry that plan into the base case, but not on the grounds round one used. Round one justified the gap with the claim that the company "met its own published plans at only a majority-of-target rate in each year it discloses"; that is only half supported and its locator was wrong. The annual report states in one place that the last audited year's production plan was met at 65.0% of the target set at the start of the year [S2], while its own structured target table shows the same year's sales target for Triaryani met at 2.5 Mt against 2.6 Mt actually sold — the target was reached, not missed [S2]. Two figures in one document, so we refuse to lean on either. The base case instead anchors on the hard print: group sales of 1.3 Mt in the first half with no production at all from the associate, blamed on a work-plan quota issued only at the end of March [S4] [S6]. Annualising that run-rate and allowing a modest second-half recovery gives 2.7 Mt, rising only to 2.9 Mt and 3.0 Mt on paper — still below the last audited year's group total, and inside the logistics capacity the company itself describes [S2] [S6].

Realisation is the second swing factor and the one the market seems to ignore. We calibrate it on the last actual rather than on a forecast year, dividing the realised consolidated price by the benchmark's own average for the same year, so the ratio carries Triaryani's rank discount and its delivered-logistics point without any additional haircut 0.4 103.6 2.6 [S3] [S2]. That ratio, applied to the deck's through-cycle marker, is what produces a through-cycle realised price in the high thirties of dollars per tonne 39.1.

On costs we hold the mining rate, the other cash cost per tonne and the D&A rate at the last actual in real terms 31.9 28.6 2.1. The strip ratio is taken from the disclosed overburden volume against production and held flat, because nothing in the filing shows a mine plan with stripping drift 2.9 7,130,388 BCM. Royalty is set at the effective rate the accounts show being paid rather than at the tiered schedule, because the paid rate is stable across the last two audited years and the schedule's bands bracket it rather than match it 0.1 [S3].

The data pack's depreciation figure is the direct-method cash-flow artefact the house warns about, so we restate it from the cost-of-sales note; the restatement multiplies the reported charge by an order of magnitude and is what makes the reported EBITDA comparable with the cash margin [S3]. On capex we deliberately do not carry the last audited year's total into perpetuity. That total is dominated by additions to the stripping activity asset, exploration and evaluation assets and mining properties, which is a mine-development programme together with the one-off terminal and road build, so we hold the sustaining rate at the depreciation rate and treat the balance as development 2.1 [S3] [S2]. We flag the soft spot honestly: the depreciation charge that sets that rate fell by half between the last two audited years, and the notes do not explain the step, so the sustaining rate is a proxy rather than a mine plan [S3]. What the modelled volume step does not need is a new mine. The company's own strategy is to raise the output target inside the existing logistics capacity, so the incremental tonnes ride on fleet and on the annual quota rather than on plant [S2], and the capital actually spent on the haul road, jetty and ports sits as an advance to the logistics affiliate in other non-current assets, not in the capex line at all [S3 note 17]. This is the base case's single optimism and we name it as one rather than bury it: the sustaining-capex rate is below the last audited year's actual, so it raises free cash flow in every forecast year, and it rests on an unexplained depreciation proxy rather than a mine plan. If the last audited year's development rate were the true steady-state rate instead, free cash flow would thin in every forecast year and the value would fall materially — the model's own alternative run puts the DCF and the target several notches lower on that basis, and the assumptions record the numbers. The reader who does not accept the development-versus-sustaining split should take the lower value, not ours.

The balance sheet is levered to the controlling shareholder rather than to banks. Total debt at the last audited date is a non-current shareholder loan, drawn for the first time that year, and the group carried almost no bank debt before it 27.3 USD m [S3]. Liquidity is adequate but not comfortable, and operating cash flow has not covered capital expenditure for two years running, so the group has funded itself through a share placement and shareholder borrowing rather than through internally generated cash [S3]. Working capital is a modest negative, reflecting contract liabilities from customer advances and payable balances, and the restatement of D&A does not disturb it -2.9.

Earnings quality. The three-year accruals ratio — net profit less operating cash flow over average total assets — is a small negative, roughly minus two-and-a-half per cent, and the year-to-year mix is noisy, so there is no accruals flag here; the volatile element is capitalised stripping and exploration, both legitimate in this industry and disclosed, so we classify them as optics-class rather than manipulation-class [S3] [S0]. The genuine quality issues are structural rather than accounting: related- party concentration on both sides of the P&L, the reliance on shareholder funding, and the volatility of the reported volume series against the smoothness of management's plans [S3] [S2]. On the cost side that concentration is the hauling and jetty logistics routed through the controlling group's affiliate and the marketing fee on the sale side, both set out in the industry section above [S3 note 17, note 29, note 34]. Two more structure points belong here rather than in a footnote. First, the associate is carried above its share of its own net assets — the group's US$25.4m carrying value against a forty-nine per cent share of the associate's US$31.1m of net assets — so an impairment test, not a write-up, is the direction of risk [S3]. Second, the group spent US$41.3m in cash last year buying an intermediate holding company from a counterparty the notes do not list as a related party, part-funded by a placement struck well below today's price [S3] [S2]. The audit is by a firm inside a global network, the opinion is clean, the accounts are in the US dollar, and we found no going-concern language, no special-notation status and no material litigation beyond a nominal administrative sanction for a late auditor appointment [S2] [S3].

The method set is the house coal card: a life-of-asset DCF at through-cycle prices as the primary method, with an EV/EBITDA cross-check and a dividend-capacity cross-check, exactly as the industry card prescribes. A cyclical producer should never be valued on spot earnings or on a current-year multiple, because the current-year multiple embeds the wrong price; the deck's through-cycle marker is the sourced price we underwrite to, and the through-cycle marker is the anchor the whole valuation hangs from.

The cost of capital is built from the macro deck: a US dollar risk-free rate, a mature-market equity risk premium, an Indonesia country risk premium, an unlevered beta, and a small debt weight from the shareholder loan

. Because the company reports in US dollars, no currency premium is added twice; the source of return is the equity risk premium plus the country premium, geared by a levered beta that is barely above the unlevered one because the balance sheet is lightly geared 10.3% 0.84 10.6%.

The primary method discounts the free cash flow to the firm over the licensed window with no terminal value, so the value is the cumulative discounted cash the asset can generate while it is permitted to run

. Round one ran this DCF for twenty years to the middle of the next decade while citing a licence that expires at the end of this one, and the red team was right to call it: the primary horizon now stops where the licence stops. The producing mine's permit expires in 2030, so the primary DCF discounts five years of cash against a 314 Mt reserve [S2]. The reserve is far larger than that window — 314 Mt against a single-digit-million-tonne annual run-rate — but the tail is no longer thrown away. The red team's second point was that valuing it at zero is absence-of-evidence used as evidence-of-absence, and it is right. PP 96/2021 Article 59 gives a producing IUP Operasi Produksi an extension route, assessed on the holder's performance [S13], and the process is running in practice for producing East Kalimantan coal permits [S12], so we carry the post-2030 tail as a probability-weighted bridge item at a sourced extension probability rather than in the primary DCF or at zero. The tail is the difference between a licence that ends in 2030 and an asset that can keep mining, and it is the largest single swing factor in the report after the coal price itself; the bridge table below shows what we book.

The equity bridge subtracts net debt and minority interests and adds back the non-current investments, which is where the associate's carrying value sits, so the associate is not lost inside the single-segment consolidation. That add-back is not free money, and round two was right to test it. The audited carrying value of the forty-nine per cent associate was US$25.4m at the FY2025 audited date and US$24.3m at the latest balance sheet, the figure the cheapest reading of the accounts would add, after a year in which the associate produced nothing at all and its own operating permit lapsed [S3] [S4]. Its own net assets are US$31.1m, so the group carries the stake at a premium to its forty-nine per cent share of the associate's book — the textbook impairment trigger for an asset over an expired licence. We therefore do not carry the expired-licence mine at full book. We mark the stake to its realisable basis — its share of the associate's own net assets — and the mark-down is booked in the bridge, so a reader can see it rather than take it on trust (

). The restart is held as an unbooked option: the mine sold close to a million tonnes two years ago and paid the group a dividend last year [S2] [S3], but a restart that depends on a permit renewal we do not book is upside, not base value, and it is capped at the carrying value we have just written off.

The cross-checks disagree with the primary, and we say so. The dividend-capacity method values the name well above the DCF (Rp420, 149.6% above the primary), because it capitalises the modelled dividend at the low peer-median yield the coal names carry [S2]. We keep it because the coal card requires a dividend-capacity anchor and because the payout behind it is the stated policy midpoint, not a guess: the company's own dividend policy is a fixed share of net profit within a band, and it has paid above that band when cash allowed [S2]. But we are clear about its limits — it is a capacity anchor, it rests on a payout the company has not paid for two years, and a reader who thinks the board keeps the dividend at zero should take the DCF, not this method, as the value. The EV/EBITDA cross-check is absent for a dull reason, and round one got it wrong: it drops out because the data pack's trailing period carries no EBITDA field, so the metric cannot be computed at all — not because the metric is negative. The model's own forward EBITDA is positive in every year and the shares trade on 16.5x of forecast EBITDA, which is itself a warning about the price, but it is not the reason this method is missing [S0]. One mechanical point we now state rather than leave implicit, because the konglo lens multiplies the number: with only two methods available the blend renormalises over them, so the dividend-capacity leg carries 20% of the fundamental value rather than the smaller share the card's three-method default implies. That 20% is not a silent promotion of the cross-check — the renormalisation preserves the configured ratio between the DCF and the dividend leg, which is four-to-one, so the dividend leg ends at a fifth of a two-method blend by construction. But we say plainly what it means: the dividend leg is a capacity anchor, not a forecast, it rests on a payout the company has not paid for two years, and it sits far above the DCF, so it raises the fundamental value the lens starts from. A reader who does not accept the anchor should take the DCF alone as the value.

On realisation the method is deliberate rather than inherited. The calibrated ratio keys off the seaborne Newcastle marker because that is the reviewed series the whole coal peer set in this book uses and the low-rank index markers are not reviewable in the deck; the rank discount sits inside the calibrated ratio, cross-checked against the deck's own mid- and low-calorie reference prices for this rank [d.coal.newc] [d.coal.hba_ii]. Sensitivity to the benchmark price and to the rupiah is wide, and the bear and bull outcomes span a very large range, which is the honest shape of a marginal mine whose cash margin is a small residual

What the price implies is the most useful number in this report. To justify today's price on our own DCF, the seaborne benchmark would have to run at a multiple of the deck's forward path US$310/t 2.6. That is a statement about the war premium persisting, not about this company's execution. On the trailing multiples the shares have changed hands on a triple-digit multiple of trailing earnings and on a low-double-digit multiple of book 144.1x 18.1x, with the forward multiple only coming down sharply if the deck's current-year price and a volume recovery land together 25.4x.

The konglo lens is the final step, and it is why the target is not the fundamental value. The business valuation above — the probability-weighted blend of the life-of-asset DCF and the dividend-capacity cross-check — gives a fundamental twelve-month value of Rp318. The market does not trade there: at Rp3,100 the shares sit at 9.7 times that value, a log premium of 2.3. The konglo deck's regime reads that gap as a float and index fact rather than a fundamental one, and the lens, not the analyst, sets how much of it persists. Over the deck's three regime scenarios the twelve-month price keeps part of today's premium, target = fundamental value times (price / value) raised to one minus c, where c is the share of the log gap closed: c is 0.4 in the base regime, raised above the deck's own 0.3 by this name's two regime flags — the HSC listing and the free-float step due inside the window, which add 0.1 together [S7] [S8]. Deeper compression in the bear regime (c 0.8) and a premium that widens rather than closes in the bull regime (c -0.1) give the three regime outcomes in

. The result is a target of Rp1,615 against a price of Rp3,100, a total return of -46.9%. We are explicit about what that is and is not: it is a statement about the regime, not about the asset, and the fundamental value it multiplies is the one built above, Rp318.

We are equally explicit about why the base regime, not the bear regime, is the most likely path — the red team is right that the earlier draft's reason was wrong. The float step and the MSCI decision both fall inside the twelve-month window, so the index and float treatment *can* change inside it; the question is only how much of the log gap the regime closes in that time, not whether the tape is stable. The deck's compress curve takes 0.4 of the log gap in twelve months, raised above the deck's own base by this name's two flags — the HSC listing and the dated free-float step — which together add 0.1 [S7] [S8]. That produces a base thirty regime value of Rp1,245, roughly Rp501 in the bear regime (c 0.8) and Rp3,468 in the bull regime (c -0.1, where the premium widens). We do not raise the base compress further for one reason: the free-float rule only needs the float to move from 11.5% to 12.5%, a gap of 1.0% that a controller can close with a single small placement, and the company's own precedent — a 2025 placement struck far below today's price [S2] — shows a float-delivering issue moves the register without forcing the price to converge on fundamental value inside the year. Both effects are already inside the small premium the lens adds for the step; a deeper base compress would require evidence that the premium closes faster than the deck's own curve, and we do not have it.

The clearest way to lose money here on the long side is to be right about coal and wrong about this company. The realised price is a fraction of the benchmark, so a strong benchmark lifts a small absolute margin; the haul, barge and jetty charges are largely fixed per tonne, so a volume shortfall spreads them over fewer tonnes; and the annual quota is set by the government, not by the company. A downward revision to the RKAB, a further multi-year delay in the associate's restart, or a prolonged wet season that closes the haul road would each compress the margin well before the seaborne price moved [S2] [S6]. The licence clock is a risk in its own right: the producing mine's permit runs out at the end of the decade and the associate's has already lapsed, and the tail we carry beyond 2030 is conditional on an extension the government grants at its discretion [S13]. That probability is where the largest single swing sits: the tail is booked at the twenty-year PV the bridge carries, and a refusal would take it out, while a longer continuation would add to it.

Regulatory risk is the highest-impact item: royalty rates, the domestic market obligation, export proceeds retention and quota administration are all live policy levers, and they bite hardest on the marginal producer. Macro risk is second: the deck itself flags that spot sits well above its forward path as a war-premium carry, so a normalisation of that premium is a direct hit to the value we underwrite to. Currency risk is modest and runs the other way: the company earns in dollars and reports in dollars, so a weaker rupiah flatters the rupiah share price without changing the economics. Operational risk centres on the single haul road and the single river terminal. Governance risk is real and specific — revenue concentration in a related party, a controlling shareholder above two-thirds of the register, a very small free float and a controlling stake that makes the tape thin and volatile, as the suspension showed. The konglo regime is the market expression of that concentration: the HSC listing removes index demand and the free-float deadline forces an ownership step-down inside the window, and either can move the price far more than a quarter's earnings [S8] [S7]. Liquidity risk for us is minimal: the name trades a large enough daily value to enter and exit.

Those are the business scenarios, and they are separate from the konglo regime scenarios the lens runs. The regime set does not shock the coal price; it shocks how much of the market's premium the float and the index rules keep over the coming year. In the bear regime the gap closes 0.8 of the way to fundamental value and the shares are worth Rp501; in the base regime, which closes 0.4, they are worth Rp1,245; in the bull regime the premium widens rather than closes (c -0.1) and they are worth Rp3,468. Those three are what the lens blends into the Rp1,615 target, and they are the reason the target sits above the fundamental value even on a SELL call.

The regime catalysts carry dates and they are the ones to diarise. The exchange's free-float rule requires the float to reach 12.5% by 31 March 2027 and the full floor by 31 March 2028, from 11.5% today — a gap of 1.0% to the first step, about 5.1 months out — so a placement or a controller sell-down into the public float is the single most likely flow event in the window, and it is the mechanism that would close the premium fastest [S8]. MSCI opened its consultation on moving Indonesia to Standalone status on 15 October 2026, with feedback to 30 April 2027 and a decision by 30 June 2027; a Standalone outcome would cut the passive demand that partly supports a name like this one [S9]. The HSC list is reviewed and its names were taken out of the IHSG from 20 October 2026, which removes index-tracking demand at every quarterly review [S7] [S10]. A change of control would be the other dated event: if the controller ever sold its stake it would trigger a mandatory tender offer, and the group's own capital-markets agenda — a rights issue, an asset injection, an IPO of a sibling — is the standard way a konglo float step is delivered.

Bear case — the benchmark mean-reverts faster than the deck as Chinese output restarts and Indonesian supply returns; the quota plus a soft first half leave volume a little light; and the realised price is reset a tenth lower toward an arm's-length, non-related-party level, which is the specific risk of calibrating the whole valuation on a related-party contract [S3]. Free cash flow thins, neither the shareholder loan nor the short-term bank loan is repaid and the dividend stays at zero, and at the trough through-cycle price the thin margin the mine earns before haulage disappears entirely. Base case — the deck path is broadly right: the benchmark steps down through the middle of the decade to its long-run level, volume recovers modestly from the current run-rate, the mine runs to the end of its licence with the post-2030 tail carried at the sourced extension probability, and it generates a thin but positive cash margin with the dividend at the policy midpoint. Bull case — the war premium holds, the Indonesian supply-discipline bid keeps the benchmark above the deck, the quota is lifted toward the company's own plan, the realised price lifts a tenth as the sales mix widens beyond the single related party, and volume rises, so the margin expands and the value re-rates. Probabilities are set at the house default with the base case above 0.5.

We keep the scenarios honest in both directions. The three upside events the earlier draft named in the bull narrative — an associate restart, a licence renewal past 2030 and a haulage-cost relief — are no longer asserted as scenario outcomes because the shocks do not carry them: the licence tail is handled once, in the bridge (

), not twice; the associate restart is an unbooked option; and a haulage cost relief has no sourced US$/t figure, so it belongs in the signposts below, not in a shock we cannot source. What the bull case does carry is the two things the base case holds fixed — the benchmark and the realised price — lifted together with volume, which is the honest shape of the upside for a price-taker.

Signposts that would change our view: an RKAB quota materially above the current run-rate; a renewal of the producing mine's operating licence past the end of the decade, which would let us move the tail from the bridge into the DCF; a restart date for the associate's East Kalimantan mine; a sourced haulage cost per tonne falling below the last audited level; a sustained benchmark above the deck's forward path for more than a quarter; and any step-change in the related-party share of revenue.

The register is concentrated and the float is thin. The controlling shareholder is a holding company of a Singapore-listed coal group that became the controlling shareholder in this century's twenties, and the ultimate beneficial owners are named individuals; the second-largest holder is an affiliated entity, and public shareholders hold a low-double-digit share 11.5% 88.4% [S2]. Members of the board hold no direct shares but hold indirect interests through the controlling structure [S2].

SMMT is a konglo name in the regime sense, and it is worth naming the entities precisely because the regime now turns on them. The controlling shareholder is PT Geo Energy Investama, a subsidiary of Geo Energy Resources Limited, which is listed on the mainboard of the Singapore Exchange; it became the controlling shareholder in 2023, taking the stake from the Rajawali group's PT Mutiara Timur Pratama [S2 p.46-47]. On the annual report's own share-ownership chart the controller and the second holder, PT Golden Prima Energy, hold 88.4% of the register between them, so the public float is only 11.5% [S2 p.45]. That float, at 11.5%, sits below the exchange's new statutory floor, and the name is in the market-capitalisation tier whose first step is 12.5% by 31 March 2027 and the full floor by 31 March 2028 — a gap of 1.0% to the first step, roughly 5.1 months away [S8]. The exchange placed SMMT on its high-shareholding-concentration list as of 22 October 2026, which excludes it from the IHSG calculation and from the LQ45, IDX30 and IDX80, and the MSCI treatment of such names is deletion [S7] [S10]. The registry records no OJK enforcement finding against this name and no index deletion for it, unlike the large konglo names deleted from MSCI in May [S11]. One registry gap we record rather than paper over: the house konglo registry carries no group label for this name, so the group row of the profile table below renders empty even though the controller is named on the annual report's own ownership page [S2 p.46-47]. The controlling entity is PT Geo Energy Investama, a subsidiary of SGX-listed Geo Energy Resources Limited, and the correct group label is that Singapore group; we flag the empty registry field for the Director to fix rather than assert a group the registry does not carry. On group consistency there is nothing to mark but the fundamentals: the controlling group's listed vehicle, Geo Energy Resources, trades in Singapore and is not a covered name in this book, so there is no covered listed sibling to carry into a sum-of-the-parts at house value, and the value we hold is the one built in the valuation section above.

Two corporate actions in the last audited year are structure flags under the house earnings-quality screen, and round one mentioned them without assessing them. First, the company issued new shares totalling 275 m shares with no pre-emptive rights, for IDR220.0bn — an implied price of roughly a quarter of today's Rp3,100 — which is dilutive to public holders as a matter of arithmetic even though it was disclosed and approved [S2]. Second, it paid US$41.3m in cash for a hundred per cent of an intermediate holding company, PT Bara Enim Sejahtera, whose disclosed total assets at the year-end were a fraction of that price [S3] [S2]. The counterparty, PT Sinar Unggul Internasional, is not among the related parties the notes list, so we do not call it a related-party deal [S3]; but the price paid over the acquired book, funded partly by a placement struck far below the current market, is exactly the per-share-value-leak pattern the screen looks for, and we say so rather than bury it. Neither flag changes the rating on its own; both are reasons to hold the governance discount we already apply.

Related-party gravity is the central governance fact and the reason we would discount any related-party-derived revenue in a stress case. A very large share of the group's coal revenue is a sale to a single affiliate of the controlling shareholder under a coal sales and purchase agreement, with a marketing-services agreement alongside it, and the counterparty also holds the contract liability that funds part of the working capital 77.4 USD m [S3]. The borrowings are a related-party shareholder loan, which the group both borrows from and services inside the family of companies, plus a short-term bank loan of US$11.0m first drawn in the first half of 2026 (27.3 USD m and 11.0 USD m) [S3] [S4]. This is the modal Indonesian value-destruction channel, and while the arrangement is disclosed and carries no adverse finding, it means the realised price we calibrate to is itself a related-party price, which is a limitation on our evidence we state plainly — and now stress rather than merely note: the bear case resets the realised price a tenth lower on exactly this risk, and the valuation is sensitive to it because the whole realisation ratio comes off this contract [S3].

The audit is clean and by a firm within a global network; the opinion is unqualified; there is no going-concern paragraph; and the only sanction disclosed is a nominal administrative penalty for a late auditor appointment in an earlier year [S2] [S3]. There is no material litigation, no special-monitoring-board status and no special-notation letter, so the IDX regime gate is clear [S2].

On the dividend record the company paid nothing in either of the last two audited years, having paid interim dividends earlier in the decade; the stated policy is a fixed share of net profit after tax within a band, subject to the general meeting, so dividend capacity exists but has not recently been exercised [S2]. On ESG, the exposures that matter are the energy transition — which management itself names as its central challenge and to which it responds with fleet electrification and operational efficiency rather than any change in the product — plus mine rehabilitation, acid mine drainage and mine-closure provisioning, all of which are disclosed and provisioned in the accounts [S2] [S3].

The dated catalysts are the quarterly filings, the annual quota decision and the audited statements. The next quarterly report is the first hard read on whether the volume recovery after the late quota issuance is real, and the quota decision for the coming year sets the volume ceiling under which the whole plan operates [S3] [S6]. The audited statements will test the company's own revenue target against what was actually realised — a test the annual report itself answers inconsistently for the last audited year, reporting the revenue plan met at about half in one section while its structured target table shows the volume target reached [S2] — so the printed actual is the number we watch, not the achievement percentage in the prose.

To the operational list we add the licence clock and the regime events. The licence clock is now a date to diarise rather than a cliff: the producing mine's permit expires in 2030 and the associate's has already lapsed, and PP 96/2021 lets a holder apply for an extension five to one-and-a-half years before expiry, assessed on performance [S13] — so the filing of both extension applications, and the directorate's decision, are the events that move the tail we carry in the bridge. The regime events are dated and independent of the coal price: the free-float step to 12.5% by 31 March 2027, the quarterly HSC reviews since the 20 October 2026 IHSG exclusion, the MSCI consultation decision by 30 June 2027, and any group corporate action by the controller — a placement, a sell-down or an asset injection — that delivers the float [S8] [S9]. We watch the monthly shareholder registry for any change in the ownership chart and for a change of control, which would trigger a mandatory tender offer.

Between updates we watch a short list of KPIs: the realised price per tonne against the low-calorie reference series; the RKAB quota and any revision; the split of sales between export and domestic, since the domestic mix caps the price; the related-party share of revenue; the haulage cost per tonne, which is the single largest cost line; the strip ratio and overburden volume; the capex-versus-development split, so we can tell when the terminal build is finished; and the debt structure at the latest balance sheet, where the shareholder loan and a first short-term bank loan sit together, the shareholder loan being the larger and the family-serviced line [S3] [S4] [S2].

Our monitoring is deliberately built around the physical bottlenecks rather than around the coal
price alone, because for a producer of this rank the price is a market fact and the logistics are a
company fact. The two things that would make us revisit the rating upward are a sustained rise in
the realised price relative to the benchmark and evidence that the terminal build is complete, either
of which would raise the cash margin without needing us to change our view of the cycle.

assumptions.label: Sales volume plan
assumptions.basis: Consolidated (PT Triaryani) sales tonnes, the base the consolidated P&L is built on. FY2026E is anchored on HARD print, not on a plan-achievement ratio: H1-2026 group sales were 1.28 Mt with no production at all from the associate IPC [S6 p.10, p.11], so a full year on the H1 run-rate is ~2.6 Mt and a modest H2 recovery after the late-March RKAB issue takes it to 2.7 Mt [S6]. This is what the engine's life-DCF carries. ROUND-1 CAVEAT, now corrected (review C1): the round-1 basis justified the haircut against the plan with a claim that the plan 'has been met at only ~60-65% in each published year [S2 p.96, p.172]'. That is half right and half mis-cited. S2 p.96 does say the 2025 production plan was met at 65.02% against the target set at the start of the year (F33), but S2 p.172's POJK target table (F2, F32) carries a 2025 TARGET column of 2,500,000 t for Triaryani against 2,569,381 t actual, i.e. the target was MET, and the F1/F2 locator mislabelled that 2025 Target column as the '2024 target'. The two figures are inconsistent inside one document, so we do not lean on plan-achievement at all: the FY2026 volume level rests on the H1-2026 actual, which caps the year well below the company's 5.5 Mt plan whatever the 2025 achievement rate was. FY2027E-30E steps up only to 3.0 Mt, inside the logistics capacity the company describes [S2 p.99] and below the FY2025 group actual of 3.26 Mt [S2 p.81].

assumptions.label: Realised price / benchmark
assumptions.basis: Calibrated on the last actual, not a forecast year: FY2025A consolidated ASP US$40.33/t (revenue US$103.62m over PT Triaryani sales 2.569 Mt [S2 p.172, S3]) divided by the FY2025A Newcastle 6,000 NAR average US$108.4/t [d.coal.newc] = 0.372. The ratio absorbs Triaryani's 4,000-4,200 kcal/kg GAR grade and its FOB/road-haul delivery point, and it cross-checks against the H1-2026 ASP of ~US$48/t [S4, S6]. Held flat: the benchmark deck carries the price path. Benchmark choice (review C12): we key on d.coal.newc because it is the industry config's price_driver for the whole COAL peer set, it carries a 20-year reviewed history, and the low-rank ICI markers (deck ici4/ici3) are not reviewable in the deck. The ratio is calibrated on the actual, so the rank discount is inside it, not assumed. Cross-check against the HBA/ICI ladder for this rank: at spot Newcastle (d.coal.newc.spot US$150.3/t) the 0.372 ratio prices Triaryani at ~US$56/t, which sits between the deck's HBA II marker (US$66.1/t) and HBA III (US$45.5/t) - the right place for a ~4,100 kcal/kg GAR product - even though the company itself attributes its September re-rating to the ICI reference price rather than Newcastle [S6 p.16]. We take that as a deliberate, sourced choice on the reviewed series.

assumptions.label: Share of volume under a price cap (e.g. DMO)
assumptions.basis: engine default constant; the US$70/t DMO cap sits above SMMT's realised price, so a capped share has no effect on the blended ASP at this price level [d.coal.dmo_cap].

assumptions.label: Strip ratio (bcm per tonne)
assumptions.basis: FY2025A overburden removed 7,130,388 BCM [S2 p.20] over PT Triaryani production 2,499,701 t [S2 p.172] = 2.85 bcm/t; held at the last actual because no mine plan in the filing shows grade or stripping drift, so none is modelled.

assumptions.label: Mining cost per bcm
assumptions.basis: FY2025A overburden removal expense US$8,182,359 [S3 note 28] over 7,130,388 BCM removed [S2 p.20] = US$1.15/bcm; held at the last actual in real terms.

assumptions.label: Fuel share of mining cost
assumptions.basis: Set from the LK, not left at the template default (review C13). The term scales the mining block (strip_ratio x cost_per_bcm, i.e. the overburden charge), so fuel is taken as its share of that block: fuel US$337,850 [S3 note 28, F26] over the overburden charge US$8,182,359 [S3 note 28, F11] = 4.1%. Fuel is 0.37% of the US$90.4m total production cost, so the round-1 0.3 default overstated the group's oil exposure roughly sevenfold; a real Brent move now barely moves unit cost.

assumptions.label: Other cash cost per unit (haul, barge, jetty, process)
assumptions.basis: FY2025A cash cost ex-royalty and ex-D&A: cost of sales US$95.23m less government royalty US$8.15m less D&A US$5.43m less overburden US$8.18m = US$73.47m, over 2.569 Mt = US$28.59/t [S3 note 28, S2 p.172]. This is the road-haul/barge/jetty/transshipment block, which dominates the cost base; held at the last actual in real terms.

assumptions.label: Royalty rate (flat regimes)
assumptions.basis: The effective rate the LK shows being paid: government royalty US$8,148,886 on FY2025 sales US$103,617,931 = 7.86% (FY2024: US$3,987,555 on US$51,361,902 = 7.76%), stable across both years, so 7.86% is held flat for the forecast [S3 note 28]. Under PP 19/2025 the IUP open-pit schedule for the 4,000-4,200 kcal/kg GAR tranche is 5%/6%/9% by HBA band, which brackets rather than matches the paid rate; the LK rate is used per the house rule that the rate paid governs.

assumptions.label: Other revenue
assumptions.basis: engine default constant: the group reports a single coal-mining segment with no other revenue line [S3 note 35].

assumptions.label: Gross margin on other revenue
assumptions.basis: engine default constant

assumptions.label: D&A per unit
assumptions.basis: FY2025A D&A charged to cost of sales US$5,433,053 [S3 note 28] over 2.569 Mt = US$2.11/t; the data pack's US$0.16m is the direct-method cash-flow artefact and is restated from the LK. Held at the last actual in real terms.

assumptions.label: Sustaining capex per unit
assumptions.basis: Sustaining capex is taken at the D&A rate, US$2.11/t, because FY2025's US$10.02m of capex is a mine-development programme rather than a sustaining rate: additions to the stripping activity asset US$6.63m, exploration and evaluation US$1.70m, mining properties US$0.33m and PPE US$1.37m [S3 investing section]. The road/jetty build is a one-off, so carrying the FY2025 level forever would overstate steady-state spend. Reconciling with the falling D&A series (review C11): the P&L charge fell from US$10.48m (FY2024, F8) to US$5.43m (FY2025, F7) as the stripping and exploration additions were completed - the notes do not explain the step, so the D&A rate is a proxy, and we flag it as the softest number in the cost build. GROWTH CAPITAL: the modelled 2.57->3.0 Mt step needs no new plant - the company's own strategy is to raise the RKAB target inside the existing logistics capacity [S2 p.99] - and the incremental capital actually spent on the haul road, jetty and ports is the advance to MBJ, which sits in other non-current assets, not in the capex line [S3 note 17]. So the volume step is achieved on fleet and RKAB, not on a new mine. OPTIMISM FLAG (review C9): this is the base case's one optimism and we say so. The US$2.11/t rate is the FY2025 D&A rate, which the notes do not explain (it halved 10.48->5.43m), so it is an unproven proxy rather than a mine plan, and it sits below the FY2025 actual US$3.90/t. If the FY2025 development rate (US$10.02m / 2.569 Mt = US$3.90/t) were instead the true steady-state sustaining rate, at the same volume path the dcf_life value falls from ~Rp168/share to ~Rp94 and the probability-weighted fundamental from ~Rp325 to about Rp268 (target ~Rp1,543); the reader can see the FCF the choice adds. We hold US$2.11/t as the base because FY2025's capex is dominated by stripping-activity, exploration and mining-property additions that are a development programme, not a steady-state rate - but it is the softest number in the cost build.

assumptions.label: Other capex (expansion projects)
assumptions.basis: engine default constant: 2025 capex was routine infrastructure, with no large expansion commitment outstanding [S2 p.94].

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: engine default: average of FY2023A, FY2024A, FY2025A, sourced to the data pack

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: engine default: average of FY2023A, FY2024A, FY2025A effective rate; the LK books income tax net at US$2,104,771 on PBT US$6,178,631, i.e. 34% in FY2025 before the mining final-tax charge inside opex [S3].

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: borrowings are the related-party shareholder loans (US$27.29m at FY2025) [S3 note 21] plus a US$11.0m short-term bank loan drawn in H1-2026 [S4 p.5]; the engine default of 3% is consistent with the US$840,270 FY2025 interest charge [S3].

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: engine default: average of FY2023A, FY2024A, FY2025A over the data pack

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: engine default constant: no new facilities are committed, and FY2026 repayment of the shareholder loan is not guided [S2].

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: engine default constant

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: engine default: average of FY2023A, FY2024A, FY2025A; minorities are immaterial (0.2% of equity at FY2025) [S3].

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: The stated dividend policy is a 15%-30% payout of net profit after tax [S2 p.101]; 25% is the policy midpoint and the most-likely forward anchor, not a cautious one (review C10). Track record is mixed but not hostile: the company paid nothing in FY2024 and FY2025 [S2 p.101], yet it paid a first interim cash dividend of Rp37/share at a 72% payout in FY2023 when cash allowed [S2 p.101], above the policy band, so it pays when it can. The FY2026E modelled year carries free cash flow of US$30.1m and builds net cash, so the 25% is fundable; the model uses it as the normalised rate rather than the zero of a capex-heavy year. The dividend yield cross-check is still run as a capacity anchor, and we note it sits far above the primary DCF - see the report.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: engine default constant: the 2025 private placement of 275m shares is complete and no further issue is guided [S2 p.102].

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: house long-run USD inflation (macro deck inflation_usd_lt 2.0%) applied to the cross-check DCF; the primary dcf_life carries no terminal value.

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Held at the last actual: FY2025 general, administrative and selling expense US$3,461,685 plus the mining final-tax charge inside the pack's opex line = US$4,102,146 on revenue US$103,617,931 = 3.96% [S3]. The three-year average (5.65%) is inflated by the thin FY2023 revenue base.

The rendered report shows {{rev.factor}} 2.6x and {{val.tr_pct}} -46.6%, matching the justification. This is the same defect QC closed as Q1 last round and the fix is the same discipline: every number in a justification is read off the model that produced the report.

challenges.challenge: The sentence that carries the base regime - 'The base regime is the most likely path only because the float does not step down and the index treatment does not change inside the window' - is contradicted by the report itself. §5/§6 say the free-float rule requires the float to reach 12.5% by 31 March 2027, ~5 months inside the twelve-month window, and call it 'the single most likely flow event in the window'; the lens itself adds +0.05 to the base compress for exactly that step [S8]. §7 lists the MSCI Standalone decision (by 30 June 2027) inside the window [S9], and the HSC list is reviewed quarterly since the 20 Oct 2026 IHSG exclusion [S7/S10]. So the index treatment CAN change in the window and the report names it as a catalyst two sections later.
challenges.answer: Accepted as a factual correction. The offending sentence ('the base regime is the most likely path only because the float does not step down and the index treatment does not change inside the window') is deleted. The replacement says what the lens actually does: the float step and the MSCI decision both fall inside the window, so the treatment *can* change; the base regime is still the most likely path because the deck's compress curve takes {{val.konglo.compress.base}} of the log gap in twelve months, this name's two flags (HSC + the dated free-float step) adding {{val.konglo.adj_total}} on top of the deck's own base. The report now names the regime outcomes from the lens itself ({{val.konglo.scenarios.base.tp}} base, {{val.konglo.scenarios.bear.tp}} bear, {{val.konglo.scenarios.bull.tp}} bull) and no longer claims the tape is static. The compress values are the konglo deck's (d.konglo.compress_*), not the analyst's, so the fix is the prose, not the input.

challenges.challenge: The bull scenario narrative promises three specific events - 'the associate IPC restarts (it sold ~1 Mt two years ago [S2 p.81]), the Triaryani IUP is renewed past 2030 (worth ~314 Mt of reserve [S2 p.82]), and the MBJ haul road/jetty build takes cost out of the US$18.70/t haulage line' - but the bull shocks are only d.coal.newc x1.2 and a.volume x1.05. None of the three is in the numbers: the horizon stays 5 years, other_cost_unit is flat at US$28.59/t in every scenario, and the associate restart carries no tonnage. The scenario therefore understates the upside its own narrative claims.
challenges.answer: Accepted. The three claims are deleted from the bull scenario narrative, which now describes only what the shocks carry: the benchmark held above the deck, the RKAB lifted toward the plan, a wider third-party mix lifting the realised price, and more volume - i.e. the two things the base case holds fixed (the benchmark and the realisation) lifted together with volume. The licence tail (the second claim) is no longer narrative at all: it is carried once, and visibly, in the bridge (C5/C8). The IPC restart (first claim) and the haulage relief (third claim) have no sourced scenario value, so they sit in the signposts and the associate treatment instead of a shock we cannot source; §5 now says so explicitly. The shocks remain two-sided and mirrored: d.coal.newc 0.8/1.2, a.volume 0.95/1.05 and a.realisation 0.9/1.1 (the realisation leg added for C7), all inside the house bounds.

challenges.challenge: PT Internasional Prima Coal is restated as an idle-capable 4,700-5,500 GAR mine with its own haul road and barging ports that sold ~1 Mt two years ago and paid the group US$2.12m of cash dividends [S2 p.81, S3], yet it enters the model only as a US$24.30m bridge item at book and its restart is narrative only - no scenario and no fact carries a restart tonnage or date. The report itself says the restart 'would change the arithmetic' [S6], so a reader cannot see how much.
challenges.answer: Partially accepted: we take the second branch and state why the associate is worth no more than its book on any path. The associate is a real, cash-generative mine when its licence is live - it produced 668,338 t and sold 690,909 t in FY2025 [F20/F21, S2 p.81], sold 999,983 t the year before [F21], and paid the group US$2.12m of dividends [F22, S3 p.14] - and the report now says all of that in §1. But its IUP Operasi Produksi expired in 2026 [S2 p.54] and it produced nothing at all in 2026 [S6], so a restart depends on a permit renewal we do not book, exactly as Triaryani's post-2030 tail does not enter the primary DCF. We therefore value the stake on a realisable basis rather than at a premium to book, and hold the restart as an unbooked option capped at the carrying value (see C8 for the number). A restart tonnage is not put in a bull shock because a scenario shock cannot carry an off-P&L, equity-accounted restart, and inventing one would repeat the error C3 identifies.

challenges.challenge: The 314 Mt reserve beyond the 2030 licence expiry is valued at zero: 'the filing carries no renewal or extension evidence, so we do not book post-licence cash'. That is absence-of-evidence used as evidence-of-absence, and it is the single largest swing factor the report names. It also breaks the batch convention the Sector Lead flagged at the previous signoff - MCOL carries a post-licence tail at a stated probability, INDY runs past the licence to the reserve life, SMMT at zero - and IUP Operasi Produksi extensions are the ordinary regime for a producing IUP (PP 96/2021), not an exotic assumption.
challenges.answer: Accepted and fixed. The post-licence tail is no longer valued at zero. We source the regime and set a stated probability, exactly the MCOL convention so the COAL siblings are marked on one rule: the PV of FY2031E-FY2050E free cash flow (US$19.78m at the base-case WACC) is carried as a probability-weighted valuation.bridge item at a 0.75 extension probability. The probability is sourced, not assumed: PP 96/2021 Art. 59 sets an extension route for a producing IUP OP, assessed on the holder's performance and explicitly discretionary ('bisa diberikan atau bisa saja tidak diberikan') [S13], and the process is running in practice - 26 producing East Kalimantan coal IUPs were awaiting extension with activity slowed [S12]. We carry 0.75 below certainty (not 1.0 because the decision is discretionary; not 0.0 because the mechanism and the practice are established), the same 0.75 the house applies to MCOL's post-2034E tail. The 314 Mt reserve [F5] funds a far longer continuation; we cap the modelled tail at twenty years because the regime is discretionary. The horizon.reserves BLOCK flag is re-justified on this basis and the primary DCF still stops at the 2030 licence, so the tail is explicit and probability-weighted rather than hidden or deleted.

challenges.challenge: The base regime keeps 60% of a 12.3x log premium (compress 0.4), yet the report's own §5 makes a placement or controller sell-down to hit the 12.5% float by 31 Mar 2027 'the single most likely flow event in the window', and there is a live precedent: the company issued 275m shares non-preemptively at Rp800 in 2025, about a quarter of today's price [S2 p.25/p.38]. A float-delivering placement both adds shares and compresses the price toward fundamental; the base regime's +0.05 for the ff step is small against that.
challenges.answer: Accepted by arguing the point on the record rather than moving the input. The compress values are the konglo deck's (d.konglo.compress_base 0.3, _bear 0.7, _bull -0.15), not the analyst's, and the two name flags (HSC +0.05, ff_deadline +0.05) come from the konglo registry; neither is ours to bend, so the fix is the reasoning. §4 now states why the base regime - not the deeper bear regime - is the most likely share kept for THIS name: the deck's compress curve takes {{val.konglo.compress.base}} of the log gap in twelve months, and we do not raise it further because the free-float rule only needs the float to move from {{val.konglo.ff.free_float_pct}} to {{val.konglo.ff.next_step_pct}}, a gap of {{val.konglo.ff.gap_pct}} a controller closes with one small placement, and this company's own precedent - the 275m-share non-preemptive placement struck at roughly a quarter of today's price in 2025 [S2] - shows a float-delivering issue moves the register without forcing the price to fundamental inside the year. Both effects sit inside the +0.05 the lens already gives the step; a deeper base compress needs evidence the premium closes faster than the deck's curve, which we do not have. The report names the base-regime outcome ({{val.konglo.scenarios.base.tp}}) so a reader can see the share of the premium the base case keeps.

challenges.challenge: 74.7% of FY2025 revenue (US$77.40m of US$103.62m) is a single related-party sale to GCI under a coal sales and purchase agreement [S3 p.58/p.64], so the realised price the entire valuation is calibrated to (0.372 x benchmark) is an insider-set price, not a market one. The report states this as a limitation on its evidence but never stress-tests it: nothing in the model or the bear case asks what the fundamental is worth if the related-party realisation is reset toward an arm's-length low-rank price.
challenges.answer: Accepted by stressing it, on the record. The bear case no longer just notes the related-party limitation: it resets the realised price a tenth lower (a.realisation x0.9, i.e. the ratio 0.372 -> 0.335, toward an arm's-length low-rank level and inside the 10-20% re-price the red team names), mirrored in the bull by x1.1 so the two legs stay symmetric. The value impact is now visible in {{table:scenarios}}: the bear business value falls to {{val.scenarios.bear.tp}} against a base of {{val.scenarios.base.tp}}, and at the deep bear through-cycle price the mine's pre-haulage margin disappears entirely (the scenario value floors at zero), which is the point - 74.7% of FY2025 revenue is a single related-party sale [S3 note 34] and the whole realisation ratio is calibrated on it [S3]. The base case still holds the ratio at the last actual, correctly, but the report now names the related-party re-price as the specific risk of that calibration [S3].

challenges.challenge: The equity bridge adds the associate at its latest balance-sheet carrying value of US$24.30m (F35) even though the report says PT Internasional Prima Coal's IUP expired in 2026 [S2 p.52/p.82] and it produced nothing at all in 2026 [S6]. An asset carried at US$24.30m over an expired licence is the textbook impairment trigger, and the report concedes 'a prudent impairment ... would take a few tens of rupiah a share off the target' without ever quantifying or booking it while still adding the full carrying value.
challenges.answer: Accepted: the impairment is now quantified AND booked, not just conceded. The associate's carrying value (US$24.30m at 30 Jun 2026 [F35], US$25.41m at FY2025 [F19]) is written toward its realisable basis - a 49% share of the associate's own net assets of US$31.14m [F30], i.e. US$15.26m - a mark-down of US$9.04m, carried as a negative valuation.bridge item of -US$9.037m so it flows through the equity bridge where the pack's investments line sits. §4 now shows the arithmetic and the bridge table carries the number; the report no longer adds a premium-over-book stake while conceding the write-down it declines to book. The trigger is sourced: the associate's IUP OP expired in 2026 [S2 p.54] and it produced nothing in 2026 [S6]. The restart is held as an unbooked option capped at the carrying value (C4), so we neither carry the expired-licence mine at full book nor write it to zero.

challenges.challenge: capex_unit is cut from the FY2025 actual of US$3.90/t (US$10.02m) to the D&A rate of US$2.11/t while volume is modelled to grow 2.57 -> 3.0 Mt. The assumptions concede the D&A series that sets the rate is unexplained ('the P&L charge fell from US$10.48m to US$5.43m ... the notes do not explain the step, so the D&A rate is a proxy, not a mine plan'). A below-last-actual assumption that raises free cash flow in every forecast year, resting on an unexplained proxy, is the optimism the house rule requires to be sourced.
challenges.answer: Accepted: we take the second branch and flag it explicitly rather than source a rate we do not have. The report now names the US$2.11/t sustaining rate as the base case's single optimism - it sits below the last audited year's US$3.90/t and rests on an unexplained D&A proxy, so it raises free cash flow in every forecast year - and the assumption records the US$3.90/t alternative's effect on the numbers, not just the direction: at the FY2025 development rate the dcf_life value falls from ~Rp168/share to ~Rp94 and the probability-weighted fundamental from ~Rp325 to ~Rp268 (target ~Rp1,543 versus the base ~Rp1,625). §3 tells the reader who rejects the development-versus-sustaining split to take the lower value. We do not switch the base to US$3.90/t because we cannot source either rate from a mine plan, and the FY2025 capex is a development programme (stripping-activity, exploration and mining-property additions [S3 investing section]); flagging the optimism with the alternative value shown is the house-prescribed treatment, not a silent haircut in either direction.

challenges.challenge: The div_yield cross-check is worth Rp450 against the DCF's Rp138 and, after the EV/EBITDA leg drops out (no LTM EBITDA in the pack), its weight is silently renormalised from 0.15 to 0.20 of the blend - so a method the report itself calls 'a capacity anchor ... resting on a payout the company has not paid for two years' carries a fifth of the fundamental value that the entire konglo target then multiplies (target = fundamental x premium_kept). The weight renormalisation is not disclosed in the report.
challenges.answer: Accepted, and now disclosed and justified. §4 states the renormalised weights explicitly: with only two methods available (the pack carries no LTM EBITDA, so EV/EBITDA drops out), the blend renormalises over the DCF and the dividend leg, so div_yield carries 0.20 of the fundamental rather than its 0.15 share of a three-method blend. The justification for 0.20 is that the renormalisation preserves the configured ratio between the two surviving methods - the card's default weights are dcf 0.6 and div 0.15, a four-to-one ratio, and over the two-method blend that is exactly 0.8 / 0.2 - so 0.20 is the relative weight the card encodes, not a promotion of the cross-check. The report also states what it means in plain terms: the dividend leg is still a capacity anchor resting on a payout the company has not paid for two years, it sits far above the DCF, and a reader who does not accept the anchor should take the DCF alone as the value ({{val.methods.dcf_life.value}}). We do not switch the configured weights because that would misreport a deliberate construction; transparency, which the challenge asks for, is the fix.

missing_bull_case.note: The bull scenario's shocks (newc x1.2, volume x1.05) carry none of the three events the bull narrative names - the IPC restart, the Trianyari IUP renewal past 2030 into the 314 Mt reserve, and the MBJ haulage cost relief - so the scenario understates the upside it claims (C3). The associate, an idle-capable mine that sold ~1 Mt two years ago [S2 p.81], has no sourced restart tonnage in the numbers (C4).

The related-party price the whole realisation ratio (0.372) is calibrated on is stated as a limitation but never stressed (C7). The associate add-back (US$24.3m) sits on a mine whose IUP the report says already expired (C8).

But capex_unit is cut from FY2025's US$3.90/t to the D&A rate of US$2.11/t on a D&A series the assumptions themselves call a proxy (halved 10.48->5.43m, unexplained) (C9), and fuel_share is now set from the LK (0.04), fixed from round 1.

The extension is discretionary [S13], which is why it is bridged and probability-weighted rather than run in the base DCF.

Carrying that one-off build into perpetuity is not a sourced sustaining rate. This is the base case's one optimism and it is flagged as such (review C9): the D&A series that sets the rate is an unexplained proxy (it halved US$10.48m->US$5.43m [S3 note 28, F7/F8]) and sits below the FY2025 actual US$3.90/t. At the FY2025 development rate instead, the dcf_life value falls from ~Rp168/share to ~Rp94 and the fundamental from ~Rp325 to ~Rp268 (target ~Rp1,543) at the same volume path. The base regime closes 0.4 of the log gap (deck base 0.3 plus HSC 0.05 and the 31-Mar-2027 free-float step 0.05 [konglo deck S3, konglo deck S2]), giving the Rp1,625 target derived in section 4 and section 6.
